i0: Most English nouns make the plural with ***-s***: *one book, two books*. But there are spelling rules (*box → boxes, city → cities*) and some common **irregular** plurals (*man → men, child → children*).
i1: Some nouns are always plural (*jeans, scissors*), and some never take a plural at all. For those, see [Countable and Uncountable Nouns](/blog/grammar/countable-uncountable-nouns/).
pn-regular.s: Add **-s** to most nouns (*cars*). Add **-es** after *-s, -sh, -ch, -x* (*boxes*). Consonant + *y* → **-ies** (*cities*). Many *-f / -fe* words → **-ves** (*knives*).
pn-regular.b0.1.1: *bus → buses, class → classes, dish → dishes, watch → watches, box → boxes*
pn-regular.b0.6.1: *knife → knives, leaf → leaves, wife → wives, half → halves*
pn-regular.b1: **Pronunciation**: *-s* sounds like /s/ after /p, t, k, f/ (*books*), /z/ after most other sounds (*cars, days*), and /ɪz/ after /s, z, ʃ, tʃ, dʒ/ (*buses, watches, pages*).
pn-regular.b2: Some *-f* words just add *-s*: *roofs, chefs, beliefs*.
pn-irregular.t: Irregular plurals: men, children, feet, people
pn-irregular.s: Some common nouns have **irregular** plurals: *man → men, woman → women, child → children, person → people, foot → feet, tooth → teeth, mouse → mice*. Some don't change: *sheep, fish*.
pn-irregular.b1: These nouns don't add *-s*, but they still take a **plural verb**: *The children **are** playing.*
pn-irregular.b2: *People* is the normal plural of *person*. (*Persons* is very formal, for example in legal notices.)
pn-plural-only.t: Always plural: jeans, scissors, clothes, police
pn-plural-only.s: Some nouns are **always plural**: *trousers, jeans, glasses, scissors, clothes*. Use **a pair of** to count them. ***Police*** and ***people*** also take a plural verb.
pn-plural-only.b1: These nouns take a **plural verb**: *My jeans **are** too tight. Where **are** my glasses?*
pn-plural-only.b2: To count them, use ***a pair of***: *I bought **a pair of** jeans and **two pairs of** shoes.* (not *a jeans*)
pn-plural-only.b3: *Police* is plural: ***The police are** looking for him.*
pn-group-nouns.t: Group nouns: the team is or the team are?
pn-group-nouns.s: **Group nouns** like *family, team, government, staff, class* can take a **singular or plural verb** in British English (*The team is / are winning*). American English usually uses the singular.
pn-group-nouns.b0.h: Noun | One unit (singular) | The people in it (plural, BrE)
pn-group-nouns.b1: Use a **singular** verb when you think of the group as **one unit**. In British English, a **plural** verb is common when you think of the **individual people**.
pn-group-nouns.b2: American English normally uses a singular verb: *The team **is** celebrating.*
pn-group-nouns.b3: Some group words are always plural: ***people, police, cattle***.
pn-group-nouns.b4: The pronoun matches the verb: *The company **has** changed **its** logo. / The team **are** proud of **their** coach.*
